newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean president agonises over apology.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean president agonises over apology.

text.p: South Korean president Kim Young-sam on Tuesday appeared torn over how best to put behind him a scandal over his arrested son and questions about the funding of his 1992 election campaign.
The way he presents his case to an embittered public could determine the shape of his final months in office, and the fate of a raft of policy initiatives, including financial reform.
Already Kim Young-sam is being tagged a lame duck.
Even though the president has not been charged with any wrongdoing, in a Confucian society the arrest of his son, Kim Hyun-chul, is a stinging rebuke to him as a father.
The younger Kim is now in jail on charges of accepting bribes worth millions of dollars and evading taxes.
According to long custom, the president is now expected to publicly apologise for his wayward son.

He is also under intense pressure from opposition parties and an aggressive media to account for the source of his 1992 campaign finance, to reveal how much he spent, and say where leftover funds ended up.
There are widespread accusations that his son, who helped manage his election victory, laundered millions of dollars of unspent funds through his business cronies.
The media had speculated that the president would address the nation on these delicate issues on Wednesday.
But now that is unclear.
A presidential Blue House official, who declined to be identified, said Kim and his top aides were still undecided over when and how to present a statement.
"The president's speech may not be delivered on Wednesday," the official said. "It could be delayed."
"We are studying various ways to present it. But it's not an easy decision to make."
The official said the president and his associates were debating two main options: a televised speech or comments for public release made at a meeting of cabinet and ruling New Korea Party officials.
Local media reports said some presidential aides were against a live televised speech so soon after one in February, when Kim said he felt "shame" over his son's behaviour.
Some political analysts have suggested the president will confine himself to remarks regretting old-style money politics and promising campaign financing reform.

South Korea's president is an all-powerful figure, and there are clear signs of policy paralysis as Kim and his inner circle of Blue House advisers grapple with a corruption scandal that surfaced after Hanbo Steel Co collapsed in January.
A weakened president was forced in January to water down landmark labour legislation that had angered unions and sparked almost a month of strikes.
Now, economic reform risks being derailed.

Economists and analysts say the president may no longer have the clout to ram through controversial financial changes being proposed by a presidential committee, including provisions hacking away at the powers of the Ministry of Finance and giving greater independence to the central bank.

Meanwhile, the president's embarrassment deepened on Tuesday after Kim Hyun-chul was photographed being grilled by state prosecutors with his wrists bound in front of him with rope, like a common criminal.

Prosecutors also obtained a search warrant to seize and examine 150 bank accounts belonging to Kim and one of his close associates, former intelligence official Kim Ki-sup, who was arrested on Monday, media reports said.
